Surah 46 (al-Ahqaf): Makki, except verses 10, 15 and 35, which are Madani; it has 34 verses, though it is said to be 35. It was revealed after al-Jathiyah.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Nothing have We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth and for a specified term.﴾

"Except with truth" means: except as a creation woven with wisdom and a correct purpose. "And for a specified term" means: a term at which it comes to an end, and that is the Day of Resurrection.

"And those who disbelieve turn away from what they are warned of" means: from the terror of that Day, to which every creature must inevitably come to its end, and they turn away from it, not believing in it and not concerning themselves with preparing for it.

It is permissible for "mā" (what) to be a verbal noun (masdariyyah), meaning: they turn away from their being warned of that Day.

bi-kitābin min qabli hādhā — "with a Book from before this," i.e., from before this Book, which is the Qur'an. The meaning is: this Book proclaims tawhid and nullifies shirk. And no Book that God sent down before it among the books of God fails to proclaim the like of that. So bring one single Book sent down before it that bears witness to the soundness of what you are upon of worshipping other than God.

aw athāratin min ʿilmin — or a remnant of knowledge: a remnant of knowledge that has survived among you from the sciences of the ancients. This is from their saying: "the she-camel became fat upon a athāra of fat," meaning upon a remnant of the fat that remained in her, of fat that had gone.

It is also read ʾathra (ʾuthrah), meaning: something you have been given preference for and singled out with, a knowledge which no one else has a comprehensive grasp of. It is also read ʾithra with the three vowels on the hamza while the thā' is sakin: so ʾithra with a kasra means the same as ʾathra. As for ʾathra, it is the single instance (marrah) of the verbal noun of athara al-ḥadīth, when one transmits a report. As for ʾuthra with a ḍamma, it is the name of what is transmitted (yu'thar), like khuṭba, the name of what is delivered in a sermon (yukhṭab).

And who is more astray (than one who calls upon other than Allah, those who will not answer him until the Day of Resurrection, and who are heedless of their calling)? The interrogative here means denial: that anyone could be more astray than the worshippers of idols.

[Mahmud said: "A question whose meaning is a denial that anyone could be more astray than the worshippers of idols... etc." Ahmad said: In His words ﴿until the Day of Resurrection﴾ there is a fine subtlety. He made the Day of Resurrection the limit of their not being answered. Normally a limit (ghayah) marks the end of what it limits, but the non-answering continues beyond this limit, because on the Resurrection too those (idols) will not answer them. So the correct reading, and Allah knows best, is that this is one of the limits which indicate that what follows, though it agrees with what precedes, goes beyond it by a clear increase that joins it to the second state, so that the two states, though of one kind, differ so much that they are like a thing and its opposite. The first state, whose limit is the Resurrection, does not exceed non-answering, while the second state, which is in the Resurrection, exceeds non-answering by enmity and by disavowing their worship of them. This belongs to the same category as what was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Zukhruf in His words ﴿Nay, I gave these people and their fathers enjoyment until there came to them the truth and a clear messenger. And when the truth came to them, they said, "This is sorcery, and we are disbelievers in it."﴾]

They abandon the calling of the All-Hearing, the All-Responsive, the One able to grant every desire and aim, and call upon something other than Him: inanimate matter that does not respond to them and has no power to answer any of them, for as long as the world lasts and until the Resurrection comes. When the Resurrection comes and people are gathered, those (idols) will be enemies to them and opposed to them. So they will be in neither of the two abodes except in distress and harm: in this world (the idols) do not respond to them, and in the Hereafter (the idols) will oppose them and deny their worship.

The pronoun is expressed as "man" (who) and "hum" (they), because the non-rational are being addressed with what applies to those of intellect, namely responding and being heedless, and because the worshippers used to describe them as discerning, out of ignorance and stupidity.

It is also permissible that the intended meaning is every deity worshipped besides Allah, whether jinn, humans or idols, with the masculine plural prevailing over the non-idols among them. It has been recited as ﴿mā lā yastajību﴾ (with "mā", for things). It has also been recited as ﴿yadʿū ghayra Allāh man lā yastajību﴾ (calls upon other than Allah one who does not respond). Describing them with not responding and heedlessness is in the manner of mockery of them and of their worshippers. A similar verse is His saying, ﴿If you call them, they will not hear your call, and if they heard, they would not answer you. And on the Day of Resurrection they will disavow your association of them.﴾

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 46, verses 6–7:

﴿Clear signs﴾: the plural of *bayyina*, which means proof and witness. Or it means clear, making things plain. The *lam* in ﴿for the truth﴾ is like the *lam* in His saying ﴿And those who disbelieved said of those who believed, "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it"﴾, meaning: for the sake of the truth and for the sake of those who believed. [Mahmud said: "The *lam* in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿for the truth﴾ is like the *lam* in His saying ﴿And those who disbelieved said of those who believed, "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it"﴾, meaning: for the sake of the truth and for the sake of those who believed..." etc.] Ahmad said: This *idrab* (turning from one statement to another) in its place is like the *ghayah* (purpose) I mentioned earlier in its place. It is a move to something that agrees with what precedes it, but it goes further than the first. By this addition, together with what precedes it, it takes on the rank of two opposites, like negation and affirmation, one of which is turned away from in favour of the other. Their claim that the signs are fabrications is far more extreme and remote than their claim that they are sorcery. So he turns away from the first claim to mention something stranger than it.

By "the truth" is meant the signs, and by "those who disbelieved" are meant those to whom it is recited. The apparent nouns are placed in the position of the pronouns in order to record disbelief against them and to describe the recited message as the truth. ﴿When it came to them﴾: that is, they confronted it with denial at the very moment it reached them, and the first thing they heard, without reflecting or reconsidering. And among their stubbornness and wrongdoing is that they called it ﴿clear sorcery﴾, its falsehood being plain and beyond any doubt.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 46, verse 8:

Or do they say, "He has invented it"? This is a shift (idrab, a change of subject) from their calling the verses "magic" to their saying that Muhammad had invented them. The interrogative hamza in "am" carries the sense of denial and wonder, as if it were said: "Leave this aside and listen to their denial, which is itself a source of wonder." That is because Muhammad could not have done this unless he said it and invented it against God. Had he been able to produce it without the Arabs' help, that ability would have been a miracle, breaking the customary order. And if it were a miracle, it would be a confirmation from God of him, and the Wise does not confirm a liar, so he could not be an inventor. The pronoun refers to the Truth, meaning the verses.

Say: "If I have invented it," on the assumption (of supposition), God would surely punish me for inventing against Him. So you cannot prevent Him from hastening His punishment against me, and you cannot withstand the repelling of any part of His punishment from me. So how would I invent it and expose myself to His punishment?

It is said: "So-and-so cannot control himself when angry, and cannot control his reins when he is determined." Similar to this is: ﴿Who could hold anything against Allah if He wished to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary?﴾ and ﴿And whoever Allah wills to test, you cannot hold anything for him against Allah.﴾ From the same usage is his saying, peace be upon him: "I cannot avail you anything against Allah." [[Agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim) from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him. When the verse ﴿And warn your closest kindred﴾ was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ summoned Quraysh, and they gathered. He addressed them in general and in particular, saying: "O Banu Ka'b ibn Lu'ayy! O Banu Murra ibn Ka'b! O Banu Abd Shams! O Banu Abd Manaf! O Banu Hashim! O Banu Abd al-Muttalib! I cannot avail you anything against Allah..." — the hadith.]]

Then He says: ﴿He knows best what you launch into﴾, that is, what you rush into of disparaging the revelation of Allah and attacking His verses, calling it magic at one time and fabrication at another. ﴿Sufficient is He as a witness between me and you﴾, who will bear witness for me to my truthfulness and conveying (the message), and will bear witness against you to your lying and denial. The mention of knowledge and witnessing is a warning of recompense for their rushing into this. ﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ is a promise of forgiveness and mercy if they turn back from disbelief, repent, and believe, and an indication of Allah's forbearance toward them despite the magnitude of what they committed.

If you ask: what is the meaning of attributing the verb to them in His saying ﴿so you cannot control for me...﴾? I answer: what he brought them included counsel for them, compassion for them concerning the bad outcome, and the desire of good for them. So it is as if he said to them: "If I invent it, while intending by that to advise you and to turn you from worshipping idols to worshipping Allah, then what will you avail me, O you who are advised, if Allah seizes me with the punishment for inventing against Him?"

[[Qala Mahmud: "If you say: what is the meaning of attributing the act to them…" etc.]] Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: There is room for objection here, because the speech proceeds by supposition and assumption. Once inventing is assumed, counsel cannot be conceived under that assumption, since counsel means calling to what is beneficial, and nothing benefits the accountable person in any outward or inward act unless it is commanded by Allah, and there is no way to know that except through true revelation. So counsel cannot be conceived together with invention. This reasoning is only complete on the principle of the Mu'tazila (a rationalist school holding that reason can lead to knowledge of God's rulings), who say that reason is a path to knowing God's rulings. For if he commanded one of the acts of obedience, such as monotheism, and said: "God has made it obligatory upon you to affirm monotheism, and I am His messenger to you," while not being a liar, then he is truthful in commanding monotheism, because reason, in their view, proves its obligation, even if he is lying in claiming to be a messenger from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is a principle that conclusive proofs have refuted. Therefore, in applying the verse according to the doctrine of the people of the Sunna (ahl al-Sunna, the orthodox majority), it is possible that the attribution of the act to them is meant as an alerting by means of a thing to its opposite, through implication (mafhum). The meaning, then, is: if I am a liar, the punishment falls upon me and you cannot repel it from me; its implication is: and if I am truthful and you are liars, the punishment falls upon you and I cannot repel it from you. A similar meaning is supported by His saying: ﴿Say: "If I have invented it, upon me is my crime, and I am innocent of what you commit."﴾ Its parallels are many. And Allah knows best.]]

The Badi' (the Originator) is in the sense of al-Badi', as al-Khaff is in the sense of al-Khafif. It has also been read as bid'an, with a fathah on the dal, meaning "one who is a novelty (bid')." It is permissible for it to be an adjective of the pattern fa'il, as in their saying: "dinun qayyim" (a upright religion) and "lahmun zaym" [[His saying "lahmun zaym" in the Sihah: "al-lahm al-zaym" is meat that is scattered and not gathered in one place so it does not fill out. Also in it: "badan al-rajul yabdun" when a man becomes large and fat. (Gh.)]]. The disbelievers used to propose signs to him and ask him about unseen matters that had not been revealed to him, so it was said to him: "Say: I am not an unprecedented novelty among the messengers" (Qur'an 46:9), so that I may bring you whatever you propose, and inform you of every unseen matter you ask about. For the messengers did not come except with what God gave them of His signs, and did not inform except of what was revealed to them. Moses, upon him be blessings from God, answered Pharaoh's saying, "What then of the former generations?" (Qur'an 20:51), with his saying: "Its knowledge is with my Lord" (Qur'an 20:52), and "I do not know" (Qur'an 46:9), because I have no knowledge of the unseen, namely what God will do with me and with you in the time to come of His acts, and what He will decree for me and for you of His judgments. "I only follow what is revealed to me" (Qur'an 46:9). It is related from al-Hasan: "I do not know what will become of my affair and your affair in this world, and which of us will be the victor and which the vanquished." It is related from al-Kalbi: his companions said to him, after they had grown weary of the harm of the polytheists, "How long shall we remain in this state?" He said: "I do not know what will be done with me or with you. Shall I stay in Mecca, or am I commanded to leave for a land that has been shown to me and that I have seen"—meaning in his dream—"having palm trees and trees?" It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: "what will be done with me or with you in the Hereafter," and he said: it is abrogated by His saying: "That God may forgive you your former and latter sins" (Qur'an 48:2). It is also permissible that it be a negation of detailed knowledge [[Mahmud said: "The best thing said about it is to take it as detailed knowledge, meaning that the detail of what will come to pass of good for the good and of evil for the evil ... etc." Ahmad said: "He built on the basis that the second genitive is conjoined to its like, and that both are in the relative clause of one relative pronoun. Had it been said that the second genitive is in the relative clause of an elided relative pronoun conjoined to its like, so that the sense is: 'I do not know what will be done with me nor what will be done with you,' then the 'la' would fall in its place without need of interpretation; but eliding a conjoined relative pronoun and its details is common. From it is the verse:

"Whoever among you satirizes the Messenger of God, and whoever praises him and supports him, are equal,"

meaning Hassan, may God be pleased with him: "Whoever satirizes the Messenger of God ﷺ and whoever praises him are equal."]]. It has also been read "mā yuf'alu" with a fathah on the ya', meaning God, exalted and mighty is He, does it. If you say: "yuf'alu" is affirmative, not negative, so the proper form of the speech would be "what will be done with me and with you." I reply: Yes, but since the negation in "mā adrī" encompasses it, by its inclusion of "mā" and what falls within its scope, that is correct and fine.

Do you not see His saying: "Do they not see that God, who created the heavens and the earth and did not tire in creating them, is able to give life to the dead?" (Qur'an 46:33), how the ba' entered into the scope of "anna," and that is because the negation includes it together with what falls within its scope. The "mā" in "mā yuf'alu" may be a relative pronoun in the accusative, or an interrogative in the nominative. It has been read "yūḥā," meaning God, exalted and mighty is He.

The response to the condition is omitted. Its implied sense is: "If the Qur'an is from Allah and you disbelieve in it, are you not wrongdoers?"

This omitted response is indicated by His words ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾.

The witness from the Children of Israel was Abdullah ibn Salam. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived in Medina, he looked at his face and knew that it was not the face of a liar. He examined him closely and became certain that he was the awaited Prophet, and he said to him: "I am going to ask you about three things that only a prophet knows: What is the first sign of the Hour? What is the first food that the people of Paradise will eat? And why does a child resemble its father or its mother?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: [[Narrated by al-Bukhari through the transmission of Humayd from Anas, and he completed it.]] "As for the first sign of the Hour, it is a fire that will gather the people from the east to the west. As for the first food the people of Paradise will eat, it is the caudate lobe of a fish's liver. As for the child, if the man's water precedes, the child resembles him, and if the woman's water precedes, the child resembles her." He said: "I bear witness that you are truly the Messenger of Allah." Then he said: "O Messenger of Allah, the Jews are a people of slander, and if they learn of my Islam before you ask them about me, they will slander me before you." [[His words "slander me" mean: they will accuse me of what is not in me. (ʿ)]] Then the Jews came, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: "What kind of man is Abdullah among you?" They said: "He is the best of us and the son of the best of us, our master and the son of our master, and the most learned of us and the son of the most learned of us." He said: "What do you think if Abdullah embraces Islam?" They said: "May Allah protect him from that." Then Abdullah came out to them and said: "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." They said: "He is the worst of us and the son of the worst of us," and they belittled him. He said: "This is what I feared, O Messenger of Allah, and what I was wary of." Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas said: "I did not hear the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say to anyone walking on the face of the earth that he is among the people of Paradise, except to Abdullah ibn Salam." [[Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim).]] It was concerning him that the verse was revealed: ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified to its like﴾. [[Al-Bukhari included it but expressed doubt about its inclusion. al-Tabari narrated through the transmission of Muhammad ibn Yusuf ibn Abdullah ibn Salam that Abdullah ibn Salam said: "This verse was revealed concerning me." Then he narrated from al-Sha'bi that he denied this because the surah is Meccan. Thus Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated it from al-Sha'bi.]] The pronoun refers to the Qur'an, meaning: "upon its like" in meaning, namely what is in the Torah of the meanings that agree with the meanings of the Qur'an, such as monotheism, promise, warning, and other matters. This is supported by His words: ﴿And indeed it is in the scriptures of the former peoples﴾ and ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scrolls﴾ and ﴿Thus does He reveal to you and to those before you﴾.

It is also possible that the meaning is: "If it is from Allah and you disbelieve in it, and a witness testified to something similar, meaning its being from Allah." If you ask: "Tell me about the structure of this statement so that I may understand its meaning from the perspective of its structure"? I say: The first waw is conjunctive, joining kafartum (you disbelieved) to the conditional verb, just as thumma (then) in His words ﴿Say: Have you considered: if it is from Allah, then you disbelieve in it﴾ joins it. Likewise, the last waw joins istakbartum (you became arrogant) to shahida shahid (a witness testified). As for the waw in ﴿and a witness testified﴾, it joins the clause "a witness from the Children of Israel testified to its like, and believed" to the clause "if it is from Allah and you disbelieved in it." An example of this is your saying: "If I do good to you and you do evil, and I turn to you and you turn away from me," where we do not agree that you took two pairs and joined each to its counterpart. The meaning is: "Tell me: if it is established that the Qur'an is from Allah while you disbelieve in it, and the most learned of the Children of Israel testifies that its like was sent down and believes in it, while you are arrogant toward it and toward belief in it, are you not the most misguided and the most wrongdoing of people?" Belief has been made in His words ﴿and believed﴾ a consequence of testifying to its like, because when he knew that its like had been sent down to Moses, peace be upon him, and that it is of the kind of revelation and not the speech of humans, and he was fair to himself, testified to it, and acknowledged it, belief became the result of that.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 46, verses 11–14:**

﴿وَقَالَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لِلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لَوْ كَانَ خَيْرًا مَا سَبَقُونَا إِلَيْهِ﴾ (And those who disbelieve say of those who believe: "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it"), meaning: the statement is that of the disbelievers of Makkah. They said: "Most of those who follow Muhammad are the *suqqat* (the lowly, base ones)," by which they meant the poor, such as Ammar, Suhayb and Ibn Mas'ud. "Had what he brought been good, these would not have preceded us to it." It was also said:

When Juhaynah and Muzaynah and Aslam and Ghifar embraced Islam, Banu 'Amir, Ghatafan, Asad and Ashja' said: "Had it been good, the shepherds of the *buhm* (the lowly herdsmen) would not have preceded us to it."

It was also said: a slave-woman belonging to Umar embraced Islam, and Umar used to beat her until he tired, then he would say: "If I had not tired, I would have increased the beating for you." And the disbelievers of Quraysh used to say: "Had what Muhammad calls to been true, such-and-such a woman would not have preceded us to it."

It was also said: the Jews used to say this when 'Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions embraced Islam.

If you say: there must be a governing element (*'amil*) for the adverbial complement (*zarf*). [Al-Zamakhshari said: "There must be a governing element for the *zarf*, and it is not correct that it be governed by ... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: If there is no obstacle to its being governed by ﴿فَسَيَقُولُونَ﴾ (they will say), then the futurity and the pastness do not conflict. This is not an obstacle, for the future here comes in the sense of indicating the continuation of what occurred and passed, because the people had been deprived of guidance and said: "This is an ancient lie," "legends of the ancients," and other things. The meaning of the verse, then, is: "And when they were not guided by it, they said: 'This is an ancient lie,' and they persisted in that and insisted upon it." So the occurrence and then its continuation are expressed by the future form, as Ibrahim said: ﴿إِلَّا الَّذِي فَطَرَنِي فَإِنَّهُ سَيَهْدِينِ﴾ (except He who created me, for He will guide me), while guidance had already occurred and passed, but he reported its occurrence and then its continuation, and so expressed it in the future form. This is the way to reconcile His saying ﴿سَيَهْدِينِ﴾ with His saying elsewhere ﴿فَهُوَ يَهْدِينِ﴾ (He guides me). Were it not for the *fa'* (causal *fa'*) entering upon the verb, what you have mentioned would be the correct view. But the causal *fa'*, by its entering, indicates an omitted cause, and it cuts the verb off from the preceding *zarf*. It is therefore necessary to estimate the omitted element as the governing element, so that by its estimation two things combine as governing: the coincidence of the *zarf* with the governor, and the verb that gives the reason for its cause. Thus what al-Zamakhshari stated is established because of the *fa'*, not because of any conflict between the two senses. And God knows best.]

In His saying ﴿وَإِذْ لَمْ يَهْتَدُوا بِهِ﴾ (and when they are not guided by it), ﴿مِن﴾ (from/by) is connected to ﴿فَسَيَقُولُونَ﴾ (they will say). It is not correct that ﴿فَسَيَقُولُونَ﴾ be the governor of the *zarf*, because the senses of past and future conflict. So what is the explanation of this? I say: the governing element of ﴿إِذْ﴾ (when) is omitted, being indicated by the context, just as it is omitted in His saying ﴿فَلَمَّا ذَهَبُوا بِهِ﴾ (so when they took him away) and in the Arabs' saying *ḥīnaʾidhin al-āna* (then, now). Its estimation is: "And when they were not guided by it, their obstinacy became manifest, so they will say: 'This is an ancient lie.'" **Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 46, verses 15–16:**

It is read as ﴿ḥusnan﴾ with a dammah on the ḥā' and a sukūn on the sīn; also with both vowelled; also with both fatḥah; and ﴿iḥsānan﴾. And ﴿kurhan﴾, with fatḥah and with ḍammah, both being dialectal variants meaning hardship, like faqr and faqr. Its case is accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: possessing hardship.

Or it is an attribute of the verbal noun, meaning: a load bearing hardship. ﴿Wa-ḥamluhu wa-fiṣāluhu thalāthūna shahran﴾: the period of his carrying and his weaning is thirty months. This is evidence that the minimum period of pregnancy is six months, because if the period of suckling is two years, due to His saying ﴿ḥawlayni kāmilayni liman arāda an yutimma al-raḍāʿa﴾ ("two full years, for whoever wishes to complete the suckling"), then six months remain for the pregnancy. And it is read ﴿wa-fiṣlahu﴾.

The *faṣl* and *fiṣāl* are like *fiṭm* and *fiṭām*, in form and meaning. If you ask: the intention is to state the period of suckling, not weaning, so how is it expressed by *fiṣāl*? I answer: since suckling is followed by weaning and is associated with it, because it ends with it and is completed by it, it was named *fiṣāl*, just as the period was named by its term (*amad*), as one who said:

"Every living thing completes its full span of life,
and every one to be removed, when its term has ended."

[The explanation of this witness was given in the first volume, page 277; refer to it if you wish. — its editor.]

In this there is a benefit, which is indicating the complete suckling, which ends with weaning, and its time.

It is read ﴿ḥattā idhā istawā wa-balagha ashuddahu﴾. The attainment of *ashudd* (full maturity) is when a person reaches full adulthood and completes the age at which his strength, intellect and discernment become firm; this is when he exceeds thirty and approaches forty. It is reported from Qatadah: thirty-three years, and its reasoning is that this is the beginning of *ashudd*, and its limit is forty. It was said: no prophet was ever sent except after forty years.

The meaning of the blessing for which he asks to be granted thankfulness is the blessing of monotheism and Islam. He combined the thanks for the blessing upon himself and upon his parents, because the blessing upon them is a blessing upon him. It was said regarding the acceptable deed: it is the five daily prayers.

If you ask: what is the meaning of *fī* in His saying ﴿wa-aṣliḥ lī fī dhurriyyatī﴾? I answer: its meaning is that He makes his descendants a locus of righteousness and a place for it, as if he said: grant me righteousness in my descendants, and place it among them. Similar to it is the verse:

"He wounds in their hamstrings the blade."

[The explanation of this witness was given in the second volume, page 578; refer to it if you wish. — its editor.]

﴿Min al-Muslimīn﴾: from among the sincere ones. It is read ﴿yatagabbalu﴾ and ﴿yatajāwazu﴾ with a fatḥah on the yā', the pronoun in both referring to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Both are also read with nūn. If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿fī aṣḥāb al-janna﴾? I answer: it is like your saying: "The prince honoured me among a group of his companions," meaning: he honoured me among the number of those he honours, and counted me among them. Its position is accusative as a circumstantial state, in the sense: being among the companions of Paradise and counted among them. ﴿Waʿda al-ṣidq﴾ is an emphatic verbal noun, because His saying "He accepts" and "He overlooks" is a promise from Allah to them of acceptance and overlooking.

It was said: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, and his father Abu Quḥāfa, and his mother Umm al-Khayr, and his children, and the answering of his supplication concerning them. It was also said: none of the Companions, from the Muhajirun or the Ansar, embraced Islam together with both of his parents and his sons and daughters, except Abu Bakr.

It was recited: ﴿Aadhhabtum﴾ with a hamza of interrogation, and ﴿Aa adhhabtum﴾ with an alif between two hamzas. ﴿Al-hawn﴾ and ﴿al-hawan﴾ (humiliation). It was recited: ﴿the punishment of humiliation﴾. It was recited: ﴿yafsuqun﴾ with a damma and with a kasra on the sin.

Al-Ahqaf: plural of ḥaqf, which is a long, raised sand dune with a bend in it, from iḥqawqafa al-shay' (meaning "it became bent"). The people of ʿAd were men of pillars (ʿimad) who lived among sand dunes overlooking the sea, in a land called al-Shiḥr, in the lands of Yemen. It is also said: between ʿUmān and Mahrah.

Al-Nudhur: plural of nadhīr, meaning "the one who warns" (al-mundhir) or "the warning" (al-indhār). ﴿مِنْ بَيْنِ يَدَيْهِ﴾ means "from before him," that is, from before his time, and ﴿وَمِنْ خَلْفِهِ﴾ means "and from after him," that is, after his time. It has also been read: "min bayni yadayhi wa min baʿdihi" (from before him and from after him). The meaning is that Hud, peace be upon him, had warned them, and he said to them: ﴿لَا تَعْبُدُوا إِلَّا اللَّهَ إِنِّي أَخَافُ عَلَيْكُمْ عَذَابَ يَوْمٍ عَظِيمٍ﴾ ["Worship none but God. Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day."] He informed them that the messengers who were sent before him and those who would be sent after him were all warners, similar to his warning. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him: he meant the messengers who were sent before him and those who were sent in his own time. According to this interpretation, the meaning of ﴿وَمِنْ خَلْفِهِ﴾ is "and after his warning." This applies if the phrase is connected to what precedes it, and the warners have already been mentioned by the statement of God, ﴿أنذر قومه﴾ ["he warned his people"].

You may also make the statement of God, Exalted, ﴿وَقَدْ خَلَتِ النُّذُرُ مِنْ بَيْنِ يَدَيْهِ وَمِنْ خَلْفِهِ﴾ ["and warners had already passed before him and after him"], a parenthetical clause between ﴿أنذر قومه﴾ and ﴿أَلَّا تَعْبُدُوا﴾, and the meaning would be: "Remember the warning of Hud to his people about the consequence of polytheism and the tremendous punishment, and that warners before him and after him gave the same warning, so remember them."

"Al-ifk" means turning away. It is said: "afakahu 'an ra'yihi" (he turned him away from his opinion).

﴿to turn us away from our gods﴾, from worshipping them, ﴿with what you threaten us of hastening punishment for associating partners with God, if you are truthful in your promise.﴾

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 46, verse 23:

If you ask: From where does the saying of His, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, the knowledge is only with Allah﴾ correspond to their saying ﴿So bring us what you threaten us with﴾ as an answer? I say: From the standpoint that their saying this is a demand from them for the punishment to be hastened. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Rather, it is what you were impatient for﴾? So He said to them: I have no knowledge of the time at which your punishment will occur, which would be wisdom and rightness; the knowledge of that is only with Allah. So how could I call upon Him to bring you His punishment at an immediate time that you propose yourselves?

As for the meaning of ﴿and I convey to you what I have been sent with﴾ (wa-uballigukum, read with the lightened form as well): what is incumbent upon me and my condition is that I convey to you what I was sent with, of warning, intimidation, and turning you away, with all my effort, from what exposes you to the wrath of Allah. But you are ignorant, not knowing that the messengers were sent only as warners, not as those who propose terms, nor as those who ask for anything other than what they were permitted to ask for.

When they saw it as a cloud coming towards their valleys, they said: ﴿This is a cloud that will bring us rain.﴾

There are two possibilities regarding the pronoun in "رأوه" (ra'awhu, "they saw it"): that it refers back to what you threatened us with (ma ta'iduna), or that it is ambiguous, its matter then made clear by the word ʿāriḍan (cloud), which is either a specifier (tamyīz) or a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). This second possibility is the more eloquent and the more correct in i'rab (grammatical analysis).

Al-ʿāriḍ (the cloud) is the cloud that appears across the horizon of the sky. Similar to it are al-ḥabī and al-ʿanān, from ḥabā and ʿanna, meaning "it appeared." The construction of mustaqbil (future) and mumṭir (rainy) is metaphorical (majāziyya) and not definite (ghayr muʿarrafa), as evidenced by the fact that they occur as descriptors (ṣifa) of an indefinite noun while being annexed (muḍāf) to definite nouns.

﴿Nay, it is that which you sought to hasten: a wind wherein is a painful punishment.﴾ Before "bal huwa" (nay, it is), there is an implied verb of speech, and the speaker is Hud (peace be upon him). The evidence for this is the reading of those who recited: "Qāla Hūdun, bal huwa" (Hud said: nay, it is). It was also recited as: "Qul, bal mā istaʿjaltum bihi, hiya rīḥ" (Say: nay, that which you sought to hasten is a wind), meaning that God Most High said: "Say."

﴿It destroys everything by the command of its Lord.﴾ That is, it destroys the lives of the people of ʿĀd and their wealth, the abundant and great amount, so it expresses the multitude by the totality (kull).

It was also recited as: "yudammiru kulla shay'in" (it destroys everything), from dammara dammāran, meaning "he perished." ﴿So that you could not see anything but their dwellings.﴾ The address (khiṭāb) is to the one who sees, whoever he may be. It was also recited as "lā yurā" (not seen), in the passive form, with the yāʾ and the tāʾ. The reading with the tāʾ is interpreted, as reported from al-Ḥasan (may Allah be pleased with him), as: "You do not see any remnants or things of theirs except their dwellings." From this is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

"And there remained only the ribs, the panting ones."

This interpretation is not strong. It was also recited as "lā tarā illā maskanahum" and "lā yurā illā maskanuhum."

It is narrated that the wind would carry the tent and the litter and lift them into the air until they appeared like a locust. It was also said: The first of them to perceive the punishment was a woman who said: "I saw a wind in which were like meteors of fire." It is also narrated that the first thing by which they recognized it as a punishment was that they saw what was in the desert of their baggage and livestock being carried by the wind between the sky and the earth. So they entered their houses and bolted their doors, but the wind uprooted the doors and felled them. As for what God imposed upon them, the Aḥqāf, they remained under it for seven nights and eight days, moaning. Then the wind lifted from them, carried them away and cast them into the sea.

It is narrated that when Hud sensed the wind, he drew a line for himself and for the believers beside a flowing spring. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both): Hud and those with him withdrew into an enclosure, and the wind did not reach them except as a breeze upon the skins, pleasing to the souls, while it passed over ʿĀd carrying the travelers between the sky and the earth, and struck them with stones.

It is also reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when he saw the wind he became alarmed and said: "O Allah, I ask You for its good and the good of what it was sent with, and I seek refuge in You from its evil and the evil of what it was sent with." And when he saw a cloud gathering, he would stand and sit, come and go, and his color would change. He would be asked: "O Messenger of Allah, what do you fear?" He would say: "I fear that it may be like the people of ʿĀd, when they said: 'This is a cloud bringing us rain.'"

If you ask: what is the benefit of attributing the wind to the Lord? I say: it indicates that the wind and the control of its reins bear witness to the greatness of His power, for it is among the wonders of His creation and the greatest of His soldiers. And mentioning the command and that it is commanded from His side, Mighty and Majestic, supports and strengthens this.

"In" is a negating particle, meaning: "in that in which We established you." However, *in* is better in wording, because *ma* (what) combined with a similar form would produce an ugly repetition. Something similar is avoided. Do you not see that the original form of *mahma* (whatever) was *māmā-z*? Because of the ugliness of the repetition, they changed the *alif* into a *hā'*. Abu al-Tayyib [al-Mutanabbi] also stumbled (*aghatha*) in his saying:

*By your life, what has appeared of you does not strike*
*more deadly than what has appeared of you to the blamer.*

[[Regarding his words "Abu al-Tayyib stumbled": in the *Sihah* (of al-Jawhari), *aghatha* means he became corrupt and spoiled. You say: "aghatha al-rajul fi mantiqihi" (the man was corrupt in his speech). (ʿ)]]

[[*Lamaqihi*: the line is by Abu al-Tayyib. He means: "By your life, what has appeared of you to the striker, namely the spear, does not strike more swiftly (*aftal*, i.e., quicker in killing) than what has appeared of you to the blamer, namely the tongue; rather, both are equal in sharpness. It is also permissible that he metaphorically used 'killing' for 'striking' explicitly."]]

Had he followed the sweetness of the wording of the Revelation, he would have said:

*By your life, what is in (in) has appeared of you to the striker...*

[[Ahmad said: the verse of al-Mutanabbi is not as he recited it; rather, it is as it is narrated:

*By your life, in what has appeared of you to the striker*
*more deadly than what has appeared of you to the blamer.*

It is not sound except like this, because before it is:

*He is the son of the Messenger of God and the son of his chosen one,*
*and he resembles them, having been tested.*

It is from a qasida in which he praises Tahir ibn al-Husayn al-'Alawi. If Abu al-Tayyib had replaced *ma* with *in*, the verse would have come out:

*He sees that in (in) what has appeared of you is a striker.*

This repetition is heavier than the repetition of *ma* without dispute. Al-Zamakhshari criticized him and required him to use *in* instead of *ma* because he believed the verse was as he recited it:

*By your life, what ma-ma has appeared of you does not strike...*

But if *in* replaces *ma* as al-Zamakhshari corrected it, it would require the entry of *ba'* (bi) into the predicate of *ma*. The *ba'* enters the predicate of the working Hijazi *ma* (*ma al-hijaziyya al-'amila*, the Hijazi negation that governs the predicate), and *in* does not work like *ma* in the correct view. So it is not sound for the *ba'* to enter its predicate. Abu al-Tayyib only deviated from that because it was impossible for him from every aspect. Yet I do not absolve al-Mutanabbi of arrogance, for he was infatuated with it and fond of rare composition.]]

Al-Zamakhshari also related another possibility in the verse: that it be made a *silah* (a redundant, connecting particle, i.e., relative-linking) like it in his saying:

*The man hopes for what in (in) he does not see,*
*and misfortunes stand between him and its nearest part.*

He said: "Its meaning, according to this, is: We established them in the like of what We established you..." I say: this verse of God Most High is distinct from this group: *And they said: "Who is stronger than us in power?" Did they not see that God, who created them, is stronger than them in power?* (Q. 41:15) and His saying: *We had established them in the earth in what We have not established you in* (Q. 46:26).

[[*Silah* is also what al-Akhfash recited:

*The man hopes for what in (in) he does not see,*
*and misfortunes stand between him and its nearest part.*

*If he withholds, then life is sweet*
*to me as if it were mixed honey.*

*The man hopes for what in (in) he does not see,*
*and misfortunes stand between him and its nearest part.*

*And the greedy one does not know to what his fibers lead:*
*will he err or hit the mark?*

It is by Jabir ibn Ralan al-Ta'i. It is also said it is by Layas ibn al-Art. The *shara'ir* (fibers) are plural of *sharshar*, meaning the scattered, spread-out extremities of a thing; it is applied to the body and to burden, and is used as a euphemism for the self, as here. It is also said: they are hunting ropes.

He means: if I withhold, then life is sweet to him, like the sweetness of honey mixed with water to remove its heat. He embedded in *hulw* (sweet) the meaning of *mahbub* (beloved), so it takes *ila* (to). Then he said: but there is no good in withholding, for a man hopes for a matter that is absent from him, and the terrors of death or the hardships of time come between him and the least thing of it. *In* is superfluous after *ma* (the relative), by analogy to *ma* (the negation). And *ma yadri* (he does not know) refers to the one who turns himself entirely toward the world; he does not know the consequences of his affair, whether it will be right or loss. If they are hunting ropes, then the speech contains an allegorical metaphor (*istiʿara tamthiliyya*), where the state of one who undertakes the means of a matter while ignorant of its outcome is likened to the state of one who sets up ropes for hunting.]]

And it is interpreted as: "that We established them in the like of what We established you in." The first aspect is the correct one, and many verses in the Qur'an came in this way: *They are better in property and in appearance* (Q. 19:74); *They were more numerous than them and stronger in power and in monuments* (Q. 40:82). And it is more eloquent in rebuke and more inclusive in urging reflection.

*min shay'in* (anything of) means "anything of [the] provision," which is the little of it. If you say: with what is *idh kanu yajhadun* (when they used to deny) connected? I say: it is connected to His saying, *so their hearing and their sight and their hearts did not avail them anything* (Q. 46:26). If you say: why does it function as a causal clause? I say: because the meaning of the causal and the temporal in your saying "I struck him for his offense" and "I struck him when he offended" is equal. For when you struck him at the time of his offense, you struck him in it because his offense existed in it. Except that *idh* and *haythu* alone were dominant over the other temporal adverbs in that.

Translation:

"And We destroyed what is around you of the towns" (mā ḥawlakum min al-qurā), O people of Makkah: such as the dwelling-place of Thamud (Ḥijr) and the town of Sodom (Sadūm) and others. The intended meaning is: the people of the towns. This is why He said, ﴿so that they might return﴾ (la'allahum yarji'ūn).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 46, verse 28:

Al-qurbān (that by which one draws near): that by which one draws near to God, exalted is He, i.e., they took them as intercessors through whom they drew near to God, since they said: ﴿These are our intercessors with God.﴾ One of the two objects of "took" (ittakhadha), the returning pronoun referring to "those who" [[Mahmud said: "One of the two objects of 'took', the returning pronoun referring to the relative pronoun, is omitted... etc." Ahmad said: The corruption of the meaning under this parsing has not been made clear. We shall make it clear, saying: If "qurbānan" were the second object, meaning "drawing near by them," the meaning would become that they were rebuked for failing to take God as that by which one draws near, because when a master rebukes his slave and says, "You took so-and-so as a master besides me," the meaning is only blame for attributing lordship to another. This is not the intended sense, for God is approached but is not approached by others as a means. The rebuke falls only on attributing divinity to other than God, exalted is He. Therefore the proper construction is that "gods" is the second object and nothing else.]] being omitted [[His words "the omitted returning pronoun referring to 'those who'" are what he made explicit in his saying: i.e., they took them. (A)]], and the second being:

"gods." And "qurbānan" is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). It is not correct for "qurbānan" to be a second object with "gods" as an apposition to it, because the meaning would be corrupted. It is also read "qurbūnan" with a damma on the rā'. The meaning: "Why then did the gods they took not help them?" Rather, ﴿they strayed from them﴾, i.e., they were absent from giving them aid. ﴿And that﴾ refers to the impossibility of their gods helping them and their straying from them, i.e., that is the outcome of their lie, which is their taking them as gods, and the fruit of their associating partners with God and their fabrication against God, the lie of having partners. It is also read "ifkahum" (their falsehood). Al-afk and al-ifk are like al-ḥadhar and al-ḥadhar. It is also read: "wa-dhālika ifkuhum," i.e., that taking, of which this is the effect and fruit, turned them away from the truth. It is also read "afakahum" with doubling for emphasis, and "āfakahum," i.e., made them liars. And "āfakahum," i.e., their statement is a lying statement possessing falsehood, just as you say "a false statement" (qawl kādhib). ﴿And that is a falsehood they used to fabricate﴾, i.e., some of the falsehood they used to fabricate.

﴿We turned toward you a band﴾ of jinn. We inclined them toward you and brought them around to you. It is also read as ﴿ṣarrafnā﴾ with the doubled letter (intensive form), because they were a group. The *nafar* is fewer than ten, and its plural is *anfār*. In the ḥadīth of Abū Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him: "If there had been anyone here from our *anfār*…" [[This is part of the story of Abū Dharr's conversion, may Allah be pleased with him, from the narration of ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Ṣāmit from Abū Dharr. He mentioned it at length.

In it: "While I was one night, a moonlit night, and Allah had struck [a veil of darkness] over the people of Makkah, so that no one circumambulated except two women. They came to me," and he related the story.

In it also: "Then the two of them departed wailing, and saying: 'If there had been anyone here from our helpers…'" Narrated by Muslim at length.]]

﴿When they were present to it﴾: the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, i.e., when it was within their hearing, or it refers to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The reading of the one who reads ﴿when it was concluded﴾ supports this: that is, when he (ﷺ) completed his recitation and finished with it. ﴿They said﴾: some said to others, ﴿Be silent﴾, i.e., keep quiet and listen. It is said: *anṣata* for such-and-such, and *istanṣata* for it (to listen attentively).

It is reported that the jinn used to eavesdrop on the heavens. When the heaven was guarded and they were pelted with meteors, they said: "This is only because of some event that has occurred." Seven or nine men of the nobles of the jinn of Naṣībīn or Nīnawā rose up, among them Zawba'a. They set off until they reached Tihāmah, then rushed on to the valley of Nakhlah, where they came upon [[The words "fawāfaqū Rasūl Allāh ﷺ" are perhaps: "fa-wāfawū." (ʿ)]] the Messenger of Allah ﷺ standing in the depth of the night, praying, or in the dawn prayer. They listened to his recitation. That was on his return from Ṭāʾif, when he went out to them seeking their support, and they did not respond to his request, and they incited the foolish men of Thaqīf against him. [[Agreed upon in meaning, from the narration of Saʿīd ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbās, without its beginning, and without his saying "and they were nine men, one of them Zawba'a," and without "in the depth of the night, praying," and without "from Nīnawā," and without "when he returned" to the end. It was also said: Rather, Allah commanded His Messenger to warn the jinn and recite to them. So He turned toward him a band of them whom He gathered for him. He said, "I have been commanded to recite to the jinn tonight, so who will follow me?" He said it three times, and they lowered their heads, except ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "No one attended the night of the jinn except me. We set off until, when we were at the upper part of Makkah, in the gorge of al-Ḥajūn, he drew a line for me and said, 'Do not leave it until I return to you.' Then he began the Qur'an, and I heard a great commotion, until I feared for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Many dark shapes surrounded him, and they came between me and him, until I could not hear his voice. Then they departed like clouds dispersing. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me, 'Did you see anything?' I said, 'Yes, men in black, wrapped in white garments.' [[The words "mustathfirī thiyāb bayḍ" (wrapped in white garments): in the *Qāmūs*, *al-istithfār* is to pass one's waist-wrap between the thighs and tuck it in, and the dog's tucking its tail between its thighs until it sticks to its belly. (ʿ)]] He said, 'Those are the jinn of Naṣībīn.'" [[I have not found it in full in one context; rather I found it scattered. al-Ṭabarī narrated from the narration of Qatādah: "The Prophet ﷺ mentioned to us, 'I have been commanded to recite to the jinn. Which of you will follow me?' They lowered their heads three times except Ibn Masʿūd, so he followed him until he entered a gorge called the gorge of al-Ḥajūn." He said: "And he drew a line for Ibn Masʿūd." Then he mentioned the words "until I feared for him," and added: "I said, 'What is this commotion?' He said, 'They were disputing before me about a mountain, and I judged between them with truth.'" Al-Ḥākim, al-Ṭabarānī and al-Dāraqutnī narrated through Abū ʿUthmān ibn Shaybah al-Khuzāʿī, who was a man from the people of Syria, that he heard ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd say: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to his companions while he was in Makkah, 'Whoever among you wishes to attend the matter of the jinn tonight, let him do so.' None of them attended except me." He said: "So I set off until, when we were at the upper part of Makkah, he drew a line for me with his foot and then commanded me to sit within it. Then he went off until he stood and began the Qur'an…" the hadith. He did not mention his saying "men in black," to the end. al-Ṭabarī narrated from the narration of ʿAmr ibn Ghaylān al-Thaqafī that he asked Ibn Masʿūd, and he related the story, in which he said, "Did you see anything?" I said, "Yes, I have seen men in black, wearing white garments." He said, "Those are the jinn of Naṣībīn. They asked me for provisions…" and he related the hadith. It does not mention their number nor the name of the sūrah. Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from the narration of ʿIkrimah on this verse, he said: "They were from the jinn of Naṣībīn; they came from the island of Mosul, and they were twelve thousand." So these ḥadīths, taken together, do not mention anything except the name of the sūrah.]] They were twelve thousand. The sūrah he recited to them was ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾.

If you say: How did they say ﴿after Mūsā﴾? I say: From ʿAṭāʾ, may Allah be pleased with him: they were upon Judaism. From Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both: the jinn had not heard of the matter of ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, so they said, "after Mūsā."

If you say: Why was there partial forgiveness in His saying ﴿some of your sins﴾? I say: Because some sins are not forgiven by faith, such as the sins of wrongdoing (*maẓālim*). [[Maḥmūd said: "Forgiveness is only partial because some sins are not forgiven by faith, such as the sins of wrongdoing." Aḥmad says: What he stated, that faith does not forgive wrongdoing, is not correct. For if a warring non-Muslim plunders protected property and sheds sanctified blood, then his Islam becomes good, the Islam erases the sin of what came before without any difficulty. It is said: Allah in His Book did not promise forgiveness to the disbeliever on condition of faith except partially, and this is from him. If there is no secret in its being consistently so, then it is only that the state of the disbeliever is contraction, not expansion, so his hope for forgiveness of all sins is not expanded. Something similar has been transmitted concerning the believers many times, and Allah knows best.]] and the like.

A similar verse is His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Worship Allah, fear Him, and obey me; He will forgive you some of your sins﴾.

If you say: Do the jinn have reward as humans do? I say: This is disputed. It was said: They have no reward except salvation from the Fire, based on His saying, ﴿and will protect you from a painful punishment﴾, and this is the view Abū Ḥanīfah, may Allah have mercy on him, held. The correct view is that they are in the same ruling as the children of Ādam, because they are obligated just as they are. ﴿And he cannot escape in the earth﴾: i.e., no flight will save from Him, and no one who seeks to outstrip His decree will succeed. A similar verse is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And we thought that we would never escape Allah in the earth, nor escape Him by flight﴾.

bِقادِرٍ — its position is in the nominative (raf'), since it is the predicate (khabar) of inna (إن). This is supported by the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud): qadirun. The bi' (ب) entered because the negation at the beginning of the verse (in the question form) gives the sense of inna and what follows it (أن وما في حيزها). Al-Zajjaj said: if you say, "ma zanantu anna Zaydan bi-qa'imin" (I did not think that Zayd is standing), it is permissible; it is as if it were said: "Is not Allah able [to do so]?" Do you not see that bala (بلى, "yes indeed") occurs confirming the ability over everything, including resurrection and other things, not over their seeing [it]? It has also been read: yaqdir (يَقْدِر). And it is said: "'iyitu bi-l-amr" (عييت بالأمر), when you do not know its way (wajh).

Among its usage is: أَفَعَيِينا بِالْخَلْقِ الْأَوَّلِ (Afa'ayiyna bi-l-khalqi l-awwal?) — "Were We then worn out by the first creation?"

Is this not the truth? (It is) a quoted statement following an implied saying, and this implied verb is the governing verb of the adverbial phrase (ẓarf). "This" refers to the punishment, as indicated by His words, exalted be He, "So taste the punishment." The meaning is mockery of them and rebuke for them, for their derision of Allah's promise and threat, and for their saying, "We will not be punished."

Ūlū al-ʿazm (ʾulū al-ʿazm): possessors of resolve, that is, possessors of earnestness, steadfastness and patience.

Min may be partitive, and then "those of resolve" refers to some of the prophets. It has been said they are: Noah, who was patient over the harm of his people, for they used to beat him until he fainted; Abraham, patient over the fire and over slaughtering his son; Isaac, patient over being slaughtered; Jacob, patient over the loss of his son and the loss of his sight; Joseph, patient over the pit and the prison; Job, patient over affliction; Moses, when his people said, "Indeed we are overtaken" (﴿إنا لمدركون﴾), and he said, "No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me" (﴿كلا إن معي ربي سيهدين﴾); David, who wept over his error for forty years; and Jesus, who did not lay one brick upon another and said, "Indeed, it is a passage, so pass through it and do not settle in it."

God the Exalted said concerning Adam, ﴿And We found in him no resolve﴾ (﴿ولم نجد له عزما﴾), and concerning Jonah, ﴿And do not be like the companion of the fish﴾ (﴿ولا تكن كصاحب الحوت﴾).

It may also be explanatory (lil-bayān), so that "possessors of resolve" describes all the messengers.

﴿And do not seek to hasten [the punishment] for them﴾ (﴿ولا تستعجل لهم﴾): that is, do not pray for it to be hastened upon the disbelievers of Quraysh, for it will certainly descend upon them, even if it is delayed. And they will then regard the duration of their stay in the world as short, until they think it was but an hour of a day (﴿كأنهم لم يلبثوا إلا ساعة من نهار﴾).

﴿A message (balāgh)﴾: that is, this with which you have been admonished is sufficient as admonition. Or it is a conveyance (tablīgh) from the Messenger, peace be upon him. ﴿Will any be destroyed except the defiantly disobedient?﴾ (﴿فهل يهلك إلا القوم الفاسقون﴾): that is, except those who turn away from being admonished by it and from acting upon its requirement.

The reading of one who read "Balagha, then will be destroyed" (بلغ فهل يهلك) supports the meaning of conveyance. It was also read as "balāghan" (بلاغا), meaning "convey a message" (بلغوا بلاغا). It was read as "yuhlaku" (يهلك) with the yā' vowelled with a fatḥa and the lām with a kasra, and also with a fatḥa, from halaka and halika. And "nuhlaku" (نهلك) with the nūn: ﴿Will We be destroyed except the defiantly disobedient?﴾ (﴿إلا القوم الفاسقون﴾).

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Ahqaf, ten good deeds will be written for him, according to the number of every grain of sand in the world." [Narrated by al-Tha'labi, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Wahidi with their chains going back to Ubayy ibn Ka'b (may Allah be pleased with him).]
